topics.title: Why don't billionaires ever sell their stock?
topics.search: why billionaires never sell their stock
topics.angle: Our Short said they borrow instead. The long version answers the questions it left open: why a loan isn't taxed, who lends them billions, what happens when the shares fall, and what happens when they die.
topics.why_now: Expands our 1,170-view Short 'Why billionaires never sell their stock' (v-20261021-05, 72% viewed), the second-best Short we have. Owner 2026-11-04: long videos grow out of 1K+ Shorts. Different from L-20261023-01 (debt in general, 13 views): this is one question, the one the Short raised, titled as people search it.
outline: hook (0:00): restate the Short in Sikka's words: 'billionaires almost never sell; they borrow'. Rohan: 'then where does the money for the yacht come from?' Picture the whole video hangs on: a vault of shares that never opens, with a pipe of loans coming out of its side
promise (by 0:25): four answers, and the last one is the reason the vault never has to open
item 1 (~60 s, reveal at 0:45), selling is taxed: sell $1M of stock bought for almost nothing and up to the top 20% long-term rate goes to tax (fact: IRS 20%; maths fee_take 20% of $1M = $200,000)

item 2, a loan isn't income: borrow $1M against the shares at an assumed 5% for 10 years: interest $272,786 (emi) while the untouched $1M at an assumed 8% grows to $2.16M (lumpsum). Board card: the two sums side by side
recap-and-tease at ~2:00: 'so borrowing is cheaper than selling. But who lends a billionaire money, and how much?'

item 3, the real numbers: Elon Musk has about 236 million Tesla shares pledged as collateral; Tesla caps the borrowing at $3.5B or 25% of their value, and says he has no such loans right now (facts, Tesla's own filing). Priya: the arrangement is the point, flexibility on tap

item 4, the year with no tax: ProPublica's IRS files: the 25 richest Americans grew $401B richer in 2014-2018 and paid $13.6B, a 3.4% 'true tax rate'; Musk paid no federal income tax in 2018 (facts). Sharma Uncle: legal, every step
recap-and-tease at ~4:00: 'and when the shares fall? the bank can sell them for you' (the risk, said plainly)

item 5 (strongest, last): why the vault never opens: the loan is paid from new loans while shares keep growing, and US heirs inherit at a stepped-up value (verify IRS step-up); the same mechanism at our size is just 'don't sell your index fund for a car'
ending: loop back to the Short's line, ask the viewer 'would you borrow against your shares?', one CTA, disclaimer end card

topics.angle: Your $10,000 in a drawer still says $10,000 in 20 years. It just buys what $5,537 buys today.

promise (by 0:20): six things inflation does to your money that nobody says out loud, and the last one is the reason the rich are never in cash
item 1, the drawer: $10,000 at an assumed 3% inflation buys what $5,537 buys today after 20 years (real_return, rate 0) — the bill shrinks, reveal by 0:45
item 2, the bank account: at 4% it reads $21,911 but buys $12,132 of today's goods: a real 1% a year (real_return) — Priya's chart: the number line climbing while the buying-power line barely moves
recap-and-tease at ~2:30: 'so a bank barely keeps up. Now watch what it does to your bills'

topics.angle: Each level of wealth runs on different rules, and the jump between two levels is a different skill each time.
topics.why_now: Levels of wealth is proven at Casually Explained 13.5M, MagnatesMedia 5.2M, Memeable Data 5.0M, The Analyst 2.5M. Our India levels video (L-20261021-01) stopped at a crore; this one is global and climbs into the ultra-rich, where our billionaire Shorts get our best views (1,100-1,180). Not before mid-November: the India levels video went up on 2026-10-21.
outline: hook (0:00): one $100 bill on a table, and the camera pulls back level by level (the picture the video hangs on: a staircase of money where each step is ten times taller)
promise (by 0:20): seven levels, the rule that runs each one, and the move to the next
level 1, below zero: owing more than you own
level 2, the first $87,047: $500 a month for 10 years at an assumed 7% (sip)
recap-and-tease at ~2:30
level 3, $100,000 that works alone: $761,226 in 30 years without adding a cent (lumpsum)
level 4, the millionaire: at an assumed 4% a year the pile pays $40,000 a year (fee_take) — comfortable, not free
recap-and-tease at ~5:00: 'one more zero changes everything'
level 5, ten million: $400,000 a year, ten times level 4 (fee_take + compare); Sharma lives here
level 6 (strongest, ~2/3 in): the ultra-rich who borrow instead of sell (a callback to our billionaire Shorts, said in words, no new figures)
level 7, the billionaire: the money is too big to spend; a scale picture, no invented numbers
payoff: the one move anyone can make: start the climb early — $500 a month for 40 years is $1.3M, for 20 years $261,983 (sip x2 + compare); 'comment your level'
ending within 30 s: one CTA, disclaimer end card

topics.title: Every way billionaires avoid paying tax, explained
topics.angle: Billionaires pay a smaller share of their wealth in tax than a teacher. Every legal trick, one by one, with the numbers.
topics.why_now: Global first (owner, 2026-10-23): our 'Why billionaires never sell their stock' got 1,121 views while the local Shorts got 26-349. Anyone in the world can relate to this one.
outline: hook: Sharma Uncle and Rohan each make money this year; Rohan's payslip loses a fifth to tax, Sharma's billions grow and he pays almost nothing. The picture: a tax collector at two doors
promise (by 0:25): seven legal moves, from the simplest to the one that never ends, and which one anyone can copy
item 1, salary vs shares: wages taxed every month, gains only when you sell (income_tax_bands for a salary; lumpsum for shares growing untaxed)
item 2, never sell: buy, borrow, die. A loan against shares at an assumed rate instead of selling (emi vs fee_take for the tax on a sale)
item 3, the step-up at death: the gain is wiped for the heirs (lumpsum, the gain never taxed)
recap-and-tease at ~2:30
item 4, a foundation: giving shares away, keeping control
item 5, losses against gains: selling losers to cancel the tax on winners
item 6, living on a $1 salary: why the CEO doesn't need a paycheque
recap-and-tease at ~5:30
item 7 (strongest): the move anyone can copy, tax-free growth in a retirement account (sip at an assumed 8%)
ending: Sharma's one-line rule, a single CTA, disclaimer end card
topics.maths: income_tax_bands, lumpsum, emi, fee_take, sip, compare
verify: US capital gains rates and the step-up in basis at death (IRS)
All illustrative amounts said as such; no advice to copy any strategy

topics.title: Why the rich borrow money and the poor pay it back

demand.title: 5 Ways Rich People Make Money With Debt (Proactive Thinker)

topics.angle: Two people take on the same kind of debt. Why does it make one of them richer and the other poorer?
topics.why_now: Debt-as-a-tool is a proven long subject: 5.9M and 1.56M (Proactive Thinker), 1.31M and 566K (Alux), plus 2.85M and 1.2M in India. Scott Galloway's 'Why Rich People Want More Debt, Not Less' (with Morgan Housel) is gaining about 2,500 views an hour on this week's market data. It's for US 20-35-year-olds with a car loan or a card balance who hear 'the rich use debt' and don't know what it means. Our answer explains and never sells borrowing: the difference is what the debt buys and what rate it costs.
outline: hook: Rohan and Priya each sign for a loan on the same day. Five years later his loan has left him with a car worth less than half its price, and hers has left her owning more than she borrowed. The picture the video hangs on is a rope: the same rope pulls Priya up a cliff and ties Rohan to an anchor
promise (by 0:25): six kinds of debt, the one question that sorts good from bad, and the most expensive debt is the one that looks the cheapest

item 1, the car loan: $35,000 at 9% for 6 years is $631 a month and $10,424 of interest (emi); after 5 years the car is worth $15,530 (lumpsum at -15% a year, show the final value only). Rohan is proud of the 'low monthly payment'
item 2, the card balance: $5,000 at 1.9% a month paid at the 2% minimum ($40 floor) costs $44,200 of interest (card_min_due). Sharma Uncle has seen it before
recap-and-tease at ~2:30: two debts that buy things losing value. Next: the debt the rich actually like

item 3, the house: $60,000 down on a $300,000 home; at an assumed 4% a year it's worth $444,073 in 10 years, a $144,073 gain on $60,000 of her own money (lumpsum). The bank still gets paid: a $240,000 mortgage at 6.5% for 30 years has $306,107 of interest (emi). Priya shows both numbers honestly
item 4, the skill loan: $30,000 at 6.5% for 10 years is $341 a month and $10,877 of interest (emi). It only pays if the degree pays: Priya asks what the course does to the salary, Rohan never did
item 5, the one question: does it pay you, or do you pay it? A 22.8% card against an assumed 8% market return (compare)
recap-and-tease at ~5:30: four debts, one question. Next: the debt that looks cheapest and costs the most

item 6 (strongest, ~2/3 in): the car payment that never ends. Most people always have one. $631 a month invested at an assumed 8% instead is $58,455 after 6 years and $946,686 after 30 (sip). Sikka grows; Rohan goes quiet
ending (under 30 s after the payoff): Sharma Uncle's one-line rule (what does the loan buy, and what does it cost a year?), a single CTA, disclaimer end card
topics.maths: emi (car loan, mortgage, student loan), lumpsum (car at -15% a year, final value only; house at 4%), card_min_due (the $5,000 balance), sip ($631 at 8% for 6 and 30 years), compare (card rate vs return, or sip vs car value)
verify: US new-car loan rates around 9% APR and typical card APRs above 20% (Federal Reserve G.19, Bankrate)
Cars lose roughly 15% of their value a year in the first years (an assumption, said as one)
4% home price growth and the 8% market return are assumptions, said as such
A US federal student loan rate around 6.5% for undergraduates (studentaid.gov)
Never tell the viewer to borrow; explain what the debt buys and what it costs

topics.title: The 6 levels of money in India: which one are you?

demand.title: Every Level of Wealth in 13 Minutes (Memeable Data)

topics.angle: Which money level am I on, and what is the one move that gets me to the next?
topics.why_now: 'Levels of wealth' is a proven long shape: Memeable Data 4.9M, The Analyst 2.5M, Casually Explained 13.5M (4:38), and Humphrey Yang's '7 Levels of Investing' is in this week's fastest-growing long videos (market-data, ~1,550 views/h). Nobody does it in rupees with Indian salaries. For 22-35-year-olds who comment their level: built-in engagement.
outline: hook (bill scene): Rohan's salary SMS on the 1st, balance near zero by the 25th. 'There are six money levels. Most of India is stuck on level one or two.' The picture the video hangs on: a six-floor building, Rohan in the stairwell, a lift that only works from floor four
level 1, paycheck to paycheck: Rohan, the month that ends before the money; Sikka empty
level 2, a cushion: six months of expenses in an FD; Priya shows what 10 years of inflation do to it (real_return: ₹2.4 L at 7% with 6% inflation is worth ₹2.6 L in today's money)
level 3, debt-free: the trap that pushes people back down a floor: ₹50,000 on a card paying the minimum costs ₹1.4 L over 15 years (card_min_due)
recap-and-tease: three floors, and the lift appears on the next one
level 4, the first ₹8 lakh invested: ₹10,000 a month for 5 years at an assumed 12% (sip) - the first time money earns more than a month's salary in a year
level 5, crorepati: ₹15,000 a month for 20 years becomes ₹1.50 Cr (sip); start 10 years late and it is ₹34.9 L - reveal at ~two thirds
recap-and-tease: the last floor is not about more money
level 6, money works harder than you: Sharma Uncle; the gains (₹1.14 Cr) are three times what went in (₹36 L)
ending: which floor are you on? Comment your level; one move per floor on screen; disclaimer end card
topics.maths: real_return (FD vs inflation), card_min_due (₹50,000, 3.5%/month, 5% min, ₹200 floor), sip x3 (₹10,000/5y, ₹15,000/20y, ₹15,000/10y, 12% assumed)
verify: Typical Indian credit card interest of about 3.5% a month and a 5% minimum due (card issuers' published MITC)
FD rates of 6-7.5% at large banks, and CPI inflation used is an assumption, said as one
12% is an assumed long-run equity return, never a promise

topics.title: RBI raised the repo rate: what it really does to your home loan EMI
topics.angle: When the hike reaches your loan, how much it costs over the full term, and the two ways to absorb it (bigger EMI or longer tenure)
topics.why_now: MPC raised repo 25 bps to 5.50% on 7 Oct 2026, the first hike since Feb 2023, and moved to 'calibrated tightening'. Floating-rate borrowers will see it at their next reset; repo/EMI videos are among this week's fastest-growing long videos in the niche (Sagar Sinha, Mumbai Tak). For 25-40 salaried borrowers.
outline: hook: Rohan's bank SMS: 'your loan rate is revised'. The extra interest over the remaining term, as one number
chapter 1, what happened: repo up a quarter point; what the repo rate is, in one picture (a tap upstream of every bank)
how it reaches a floating loan: the external benchmark, the bank's spread, the reset date (Sharma has lived through 2022-23)
the setup: a ₹50 lakh, 20-year loan at 8.50% vs 8.75%
split: old EMI vs new EMI, the monthly difference looks small
reveal: the same difference over 240 months, total interest side by side
chapter 2, the trap: banks often stretch the tenure instead of raising the EMI; calendar flipping the extra months
towers: total interest if the EMI rises vs if the tenure stretches
Priya: why the 'free' option is the expensive one
chapter 3, the other side: savers; an FD at a higher rate, lumpsum over five years
what to do: check your reset date, ask the bank which option they applied, choose EMI over tenure if the budget allows
checklist recap, three steps
end
topics.maths: two emi (same amount and months, 8.50% vs 8.75%) for the EMI rise and total interest; a third emi with the higher rate at a longer months count is NOT computable yet (tenure needs solving) - either show only the EMI-rise path, or wait for the loan_prepay/tenure kind (backlog 2026-10-18-maths-loan-tenure); two lumpsum for the FD side
topics.facts_hint: repo 5.25% -> 5.50% on 7 Oct 2026; confirm on the RBI monetary policy statement at rbi.org.in before using as a sourced fact
verify: Repo rate 5.50% from 5.25% on 7 Oct 2026, on rbi.org.in
That repo-linked (EBLR) home loans reset at least every three months per RBI rules
Typical home loan rates near 8.5% at the time of writing
That banks may extend tenure rather than raise EMI on a rate rise, and RBI's 2023 rule letting borrowers choose

topics.title: Only paying the minimum on your credit card: what it really costs you
topics.angle: How long a $5,000 card balance takes to clear on minimum payments at about 22% APR, what it costs in total, and what a fixed payment that clears it in three years changes
topics.why_now: 'Federal Reserve issues warning to every homeowner with a credit card' is the fastest-growing long video in the niche this week (~13.4k views/hour) and 'What happens if you never pay your credit card' is also climbing (~1.5k/h). The CFPB says the share of US cardholders paying only the minimum in 2024 was the highest since at least 2015. Evergreen, global (USD), and fully computable with card_min_due + emi. For 20-35 viewers carrying a balance.
outline: hook: Rohan's card statement, first frame: 'Minimum due $150'. He pays it and feels fine. The stake on screen within 5 s: this $5,000 will cost him about twice that
the promise (20-30 s): by the end you'll know how long, how much, and the one number on your statement that fixes it
chapter 1, the treadmill (the one picture): Rohan jogs, the belt is interest; each payment is a step, the belt moves almost as fast
how the minimum is worked out: a small slice of the balance, so it shrinks as the balance shrinks (Priya draws it)
a year of it: paid vs still owed after 12 months (card_min_due year-one figures); Rohan: 'I paid that much and still owe THAT?'
tease: 'and that's the good year'
chapter 2, the long tail: balance curve over the full payoff, months counted up; reveal the years and total paid
Sharma has seen it before: interest charged from the day you swipe, fees on top, so the real cost is higher than our clean maths
chapter 3, the turn (best moment, about two thirds in): same balance, fixed payment that clears it in 3 years (emi); side by side: years and interest saved
the number on your statement: US statements show how long minimums take and the payment to clear it in 3 years (verify); Priya circles it
what to do: pay the fixed amount, stop new spending on the card, automate it; checklist
Sikka cheers the payoff date; recap of the three figures
disclaimer
